scenario.name: Volatility Foundation, SANS FOR526 & Elastic DFIR — Volatility 3 windows.malfind, psscan vs pslist & Kernel Callbacks Memory Forensics
scenario.overview: Imagine a forensic detective freezing a busy courthouse in mid-motion to perform three surgical checks on the frozen rooms. First, the detective checks the floor-seating ledger for armed strangers sitting in unbacked private booths disguised in clerk robes; second, the detective compares the official front-desk attendance list against a physical walk through every hallway to catch a hidden worker who erased their own name; third, the detective inspects the master courthouse bell-pull board to spot silent security bells that were tampered with or replaced. In this scenario (T1055, Volatility Foundation, SANS FOR526 & Elastic DFIR, Volatility 3 windows.malfind, psscan vs pslist & Kernel Callbacks Memory Forensics), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: volatility 3 windows.malfind, then direct Kernel Object Manipulation Detection, then kernel Notification Callback. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Volatility 3 windows.malfind, then Direct Kernel Object Manipulation Detection, then Kernel Notification Callback, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates process, authentication, and network telemetry for T1055 across the documented kill chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Volatility 3 windows.malfind & windows.vadinfo — Unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE VAD Detection
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1055 - Process Injection: Unbacked RWX VAD Region)
stages.description: Walking through the courthouse room-assignment trees, the detective spotlights a private booth inside a trusted clerk office that has both writing and execution permissions turned on yet matches no official blueprint file on the shelf, revealing an executable payload hiding directly inside live workspace memory. Running vol -f memdump.raw windows.malfind walks the kernel MMVAD (_MMVAD_SHORT / _MMVAD) balanced tree for every process. In svchost.exe (PID 2480), malfind flags a private memory region (PrivateMemory=1, Tag=VadS, Protection=PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE) with no backing file object (FileObject=None) whose first bytes contain an MZ / PE header (4D 5A 90 00) and a 64-bit function prologue (48 89 5C 24 08) (logged in Memory Scan Event 64 with VolatilityPlugin=windows.malfind + windows.ldrmodules, TargetProcess=svchost.exe , PID 2480, VadTagAndProtection=VadS | PrivateMemory=1 | PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, InjectedHeaderMagic=4D 5A 90 00 , Reflectively Mapped PE so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes vol.py -f memdump.raw windows.malfind --pid 2480 --dump (which Runs the Volatility 3 memory forensics analyzer against a captured physical RAM image , memory.dmp to walk kernel EPROCESS structures, Virtual Addr so that detects fileless process hollowing, unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE , RWX shellcode regions, MZ/PE headers , 4D 5A in private memory, and malicious Ring-0 kernel callbacks , T1055 during "Volatility 3 windows.malfind & windows.vadinfo, Unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE VAD Detection"). Next, the follow-up artifact vol.py -f memdump.raw windows.vadinfo --pid 2480 runs (which Runs the Volatility 3 memory forensics analyzer against a captured physical RAM image , memory.dmp to walk kernel EPROCESS structures, Virtual Addr so that detects fileless process hollowing, unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE , RWX shellcode regions, MZ/PE headers , 4D 5A in private memory, and malicious Ring-0 kernel callbacks , T1055 during "Volatility 3 windows.malfind & windows.vadinfo, Unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE VAD Detection"). stages.title: Stage 2: Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) Detection — windows.pslist vs windows.psscan
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1014 - Rootkit: DKOM EPROCESS ActiveProcessLinks Unlinking)
stages.description: Next, the detective holds the official front-desk employee chain in one hand while physically sweeping every office chair in the building with the other. One rogue loader erased its own link from the front-desk chain so ordinary roll calls skip straight past it, yet the physical chair sweep catches it sitting in plain sight. To hide a user-mode loader (kworker_win.exe, PID 5912) from Task Manager and Get-Process, a kernel driver unlinks its _EPROCESS structure from the doubly linked Nt!PsActiveProcessHead (ActiveProcessLinks.Flink / Blink). While windows.pslist (which walks ActiveProcessLinks) does not show PID 5912, windows.psscan scans physical memory pool allocations for the "Proc" pool tag and _EPROCESS structures, immediately exposing the unlinked running process (logged in Memory Scan Event 5912 with VolatilityPlugin=windows.psscan vs windows.pslist Cross-View Diff, HiddenProcess=kworker_win.exe , PID 5912, Active Threads=4, ExitTime=N/A, PhysicalPoolOffset=0xffffa80149201080, RootkitTechnique=DKOM ActiveProcessLinks.Flink/Blink Unlinking so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Next, the follow-up artifact vol.py -f memdump.raw windows.psscan # Scans physical RAM pool headers for _EPROCESS objects runs (which Runs the Volatility 3 memory forensics analyzer against a captured physical RAM image , memory.dmp to walk kernel EPROCESS structures, Virtual Addr so that detects fileless process hollowing, unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE , RWX shellcode regions, MZ/PE headers , 4D 5A in private memory, and malicious Ring-0 kernel callbacks , T1014 during "Direct Kernel Object Manipulation , DKOM Detection, windows.pslist vs windows.psscan"). steps.howItWorksInPractice: Under the hood, the observed step executes vol.py -f memdump.raw windows.pslist # Walks Nt!PsActiveProcessHead doubly-linked list (which Runs the Volatility 3 memory forensics analyzer against a captured physical RAM image , memory.dmp to walk kernel EPROCESS structures, Virtual Addr so that detects fileless process hollowing, unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE , RWX shellcode regions, MZ/PE headers , 4D 5A in private memory, and malicious Ring-0 kernel callbacks , T1014 during "Direct Kernel Object Manipulation , DKOM Detection, windows.pslist vs windows.psscan"). Next, the follow-up artifact vol.py -f memdump.raw windows.psscan # Scans physical RAM pool headers for _EPROCESS objects runs (which Runs the Volatility 3 memory forensics analyzer against a captured physical RAM image , memory.dmp to walk kernel EPROCESS structures, Virtual Addr so that detects fileless process hollowing, unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE , RWX shellcode regions, MZ/PE headers , 4D 5A in private memory, and malicious Ring-0 kernel callbacks , T1014 during "Direct Kernel Object Manipulation , DKOM Detection, windows.pslist vs windows.psscan").
steps.diagramAlignment: On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 across the topology from Raw RAM Image , memdump.raw and Volatility 3 DTB & PDB Layer toward windows.malfind , RWX VADs and pslist vs psscan EPROCESS.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Documented in Memory Scan Event 5912 (recording VolatilityPlugin=windows.psscan vs windows.pslist Cross-View Diff, HiddenProcess=kworker_win.exe , PID 5912, Active Threads=4, ExitTime=N/A, PhysicalPoolOffset=0xffffa80149201080, RootkitTechnique=DKOM ActiveProcessLinks.Flink/Blink Unlinking under T1014): Always cross-compare windows.pslist against windows.psscan (and windows.thrdproc / ETHREAD scheduling lists, since the Windows kernel scheduler threads must remain linked to execute on a CPU).

steps.plainTitle: Kernel Notification Callback & Driver Inspection (windows.callbacks & windows.driverscan)
steps.storyAnalogy: Finally, the detective opens the wooden panel behind the courthouse master bell-pull board and traces every wire back to its owner, verifying whether any rogue driver snipped the security alarm bells or wired its own silent bell onto the courthouse nervous system.
steps.simpleExplanation: Running vol -f memdump.raw windows.callbacks and windows.driverscan enumerates kernel PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, PspCreateThreadNotifyRoutine, and ObRegisterCallbacks arrays, identifying an unknown kernel address (0xfffff8046b912400) pointing into an unbacked kernel pool allocation that intercepts process creation events (logged in Memory Scan Event 300 with VolatilityPlugin=windows.callbacks + windows.driverscan, KernelArray=Nt!PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, CallbackPointer=0xfffff8046b912400 , Module=UNKNOWN so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Under the hood, the observed step executes vol.py -f memdump.raw windows.callbacks (which Runs the Volatility 3 memory forensics analyzer against a captured physical RAM image , memory.dmp to walk kernel EPROCESS structures, Virtual Addr so that detects fileless process hollowing, unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE , RWX shellcode regions, MZ/PE headers , 4D 5A in private memory, and malicious Ring-0 kernel callbacks , T1562.001 during "Kernel Notification Callback & Driver Inspection , windows.callbacks & windows.driverscan"). Next, the follow-up artifact vol.py -f memdump.raw windows.driverscan runs (which Runs the Volatility 3 memory forensics analyzer against a captured physical RAM image , memory.dmp to walk kernel EPROCESS structures, Virtual Addr so that detects fileless process hollowing, unbacked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE , RWX shellcode regions, MZ/PE headers , 4D 5A in private memory, and malicious Ring-0 kernel callbacks , T1562.001 during "Kernel Notification Callback & Driver Inspection , windows.callbacks & windows.driverscan").

steps.detectionAndEvidence: Documented in Memory Scan Event 300 (recording VolatilityPlugin=windows.callbacks + windows.driverscan, KernelArray=Nt!PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, CallbackPointer=0xfffff8046b912400 , Module=UNKNOWN under T1562.001): Enforce Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI / Memory Integrity) and Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist so unsigned or vulnerable kernel drivers cannot modify kernel callback arrays.
